Simulation
Collisions — Momentum & Energy (guided inquiry)
Concept
Momentum Σmv is conserved in EVERY collision; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic ones — the lost KE becomes heat and deformation.
Serves
Apply momentum conservation; distinguish elastic from inelastic; read ΔKE = −½μ(1−e²)u²rel; check Galilean frame invariance of ΔKE.
Inquiry
Equal masses, +2/−2 m/s, they stick. Do they stop because momentum was destroyed with the lost KE — or was momentum zero all along?
Misconception
If kinetic energy disappears when objects stick, momentum must disappear too.

Collisions — Momentum & Energy

Guided Inquiry

1 · Run — stick and read the table

Press Play in Inelastic (e = 0). Watch the carts merge. Read the Momentum & energy table: Σp is equal before and after, but ΣKE is not.

2 · Predict — why do they stop?

Equal masses, +2 / −2 m/s, they stick. What happens?

3 · Restitution e

Sweep the Restitution e slider from 0 → 1. Watch ΔKE shrink as ½μ(1−e²)u²rel → 0. At e = 1 the collision is elastic.

4 · Frame beat — COM frame

Drag Frame velocity vb to equal vcm (read it in Frame invariants). In the COM frame, sticking means both carts stop. ΔKE reads the same in every frame.

5 · Explore

  • Elastic, equal masses: the velocities swap.
  • Heavy-on-light: set m₁ = 5, m₂ = 0.5, u₂ = 0 — watch v₂′ → 2u₁.
  • Explosion: the reverse of sticking — stored energy Q → KE, but Σp is still 0.

6 · Synthesise

Momentum is conserved in every collision. Kinetic energy is conserved only when elastic. ΔKE is frame-invariant. Open ∑ Formal for the algebra. Hit Finish to explore freely.

Collisions — Momentum & Energy

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Two carts on a line meet, and the sim shows what each cart does and what two running totals do before and after: the momentum Σp and the kinetic energy ΣKE. The carts can stick or bounce, a single body can explode, and you can view the event from a moving frame.

What you'll learn

  • What Σp and ΣKE do across a collision, and how that depends on the kind of collision.
  • How the restitution e and the masses decide the velocities that leave the collision.
  • How the picture changes, and what stays the same, when you move to another frame.
Two carts and the contact point between them. Each arrow shows a cart's velocity before the collision.

What's on screen

  • Carts: cart 1 in cyan and cart 2 in amber, each with its mass and velocity written under it. A heavier cart is drawn larger.
  • Velocity arrow in the cart's colour, longer for a faster cart and pointing the way it moves. Right is positive.
  • Merged cart M in violet, shown when the carts stick and for the body that explodes.
  • Labels: the frame at top left, the collision type at top right, and "before" or "after" at bottom left.
See itPress Play and watch the carts approach. Watch for: the two carts moving toward the dashed centre mark, and the numbers in the Momentum & energy table.

03

Total momentum is the same before and after every collision

Each cart has momentum p = mv, with velocity positive to the right. The total Σp = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ has the same value just after the collision as just before it.

m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v₁′ + m₂v₂′
Momentum before = momentum after (a prime marks the velocity after).

During contact each cart pushes on the other with a force of the same size in the opposite direction, for the same time. One gains exactly the momentum the other loses. This holds for any masses and any type of collision, as long as nothing outside the pair pushes on them.

If the carts stick, this alone gives their common velocity, v′ = Σp / (m₁ + m₂). At the opening setup Σp = 1 × (+2) + 1 × (−2) = 0 kg·m/s, so the merged cart has v′ = 0 and both carts stop.

See itPress Play and watch the carts meet. Watch for: the carts merging at the centre and stopping, with Σp reading 0.000 before and after in the Momentum & energy table.
04

Kinetic energy is lost unless the collision is elastic

The restitution e is the speed of separation divided by the speed of approach: e = (v₂′ − v₁′) / (v₁ − v₂). The kinetic energy change then depends only on e and on how fast the carts close on each other:

ΔKE = −½ μ (1 − e²)(v₁ − v₂)²
μ = m₁m₂ / (m₁ + m₂) is the reduced mass.

The loss is largest at e = 0, where the carts stick, and zero at e = 1, an elastic collision. The missing energy becomes heat and deformation, which the sim does not draw. Dragging e up to 1 switches the type to Elastic.

At the opening setup μ = 0.5 kg and v₁ − v₂ = 4 m/s. At e = 0 the loss is 4.0 J, which is all of the ΣKE. At e = 0.5 it is 3.0 J: the carts bounce apart at −1.0 and +1.0 m/s, and 1.0 J of the 4.0 J remains.

See itPress Play and watch the carts bounce apart. Watch for: the carts leaving at ±1.0 m/s, ΣKE falling from 4.000 to 1.000 J in the table, and ΔKE reading −3.000 J.
05

Elastic collisions also conserve kinetic energy

At e = 1 both Σp and ΣKE are conserved, and the two conditions fix both final velocities:

v₁′ = [(m₁ − m₂)v₁ + 2m₂v₂] / (m₁ + m₂)
v₂′ = [(m₂ − m₁)v₂ + 2m₁v₁] / (m₁ + m₂)

With equal masses the carts simply exchange velocities. At the opening setup cart 1 leaves at −2.0 m/s and cart 2 at +2.0 m/s, and ΣKE stays 4.0 J.

A heavy cart hitting a light one at rest hardly slows down. With m₁ = 5 kg, m₂ = 0.5 kg, v₁ = +2.0 m/s and v₂ = 0, the carts leave at +1.64 and +3.64 m/s. As m₁/m₂ grows, the light cart's speed approaches 2v₁.

See itPress Play and watch two equal carts collide. Watch for: the carts bouncing back with their velocities exchanged, −2.0 and +2.0 m/s, and ΣKE unchanged at 4.000 J.
See itNow watch a heavy cart hit a light one at rest. Watch for: the light cart 2 shooting off at +3.64 m/s while the heavy cart 1 keeps going at +1.64 m/s.
06

An explosion turns stored energy into motion

In Explosion, one body of mass M = m₁ + m₂ sits at rest and splits into pieces A (m₁) and B (m₂). Nothing outside pushes on it, so Σp stays 0 and the pieces leave with equal and opposite momenta. The released energy Q becomes their kinetic energy.

p* = √(2μQ), vA = +p* / m₁, vB = −p* / m₂
Setting p*²/2m₁ + p*²/2m₂ = Q gives p*.

The lighter piece moves faster, because the same momentum divided by a smaller mass is a larger velocity. With m₁ = 1 kg, m₂ = 3 kg and Q = 4 J, μ = 0.75 kg and p* = 2.449 kg·m/s. Piece A leaves at +2.45 m/s with 3.0 J, and piece B at −0.82 m/s with 1.0 J.

See itPress Play and watch the body split. Watch for: piece A leaving at +2.45 m/s, piece B at −0.82 m/s, ΣKE going from 0 to 4.000 J and Σp staying 0.000.
07

The value of Σp depends on the frame, but ΔKE does not

Frame velocity vb shows the same collision from a frame moving at vb: each velocity v becomes v − vb. Σp shifts by the same amount before and after, so it is still conserved, and ΔKE depends only on the velocity difference v₁ − v₂, so it does not change at all.

Choose vb equal to the centre-of-mass velocity vcm = Σp / (m₁ + m₂). In that frame Σp = 0 before and after, and carts that stick end at rest.

Take m₁ = m₂ = 1 kg, v₁ = +3 and v₂ = −1 m/s, with the carts sticking. Then vcm = +1 m/s. In the lab frame the carts leave together at +1 m/s and ΣKE falls from 5 J to 1 J. At vb = +1 m/s the carts approach at +2 and −2 m/s and end at rest, with ΣKE falling from 4 J to 0. ΔKE is −4.0 J in both.

See itPress Play and watch from the moving frame. Watch for: the merged cart M sitting at rest, Σp reading 0.000 before and after, and ΔKE reading −4.000 J, the same as in the lab frame.
08

Where it matters

  • Car crashes. Two cars that lock together are close to an e = 0 collision. Σp fixes their common velocity, and the lost kinetic energy goes into bending metal. Crumple zones spread that out over a longer time.
  • The ballistic pendulum. A bullet that stays in a block obeys mv = (m + M)v′. The swing that follows gives v′, and from it the speed of the bullet.
  • Recoil. A gun and its bullet, or the stages of a rocket, start at rest and separate. Σp stays zero, so the lighter part moves faster.
  • Where it stops working. The sim is head-on and one-dimensional. Real collisions can glance, spin the bodies and last a finite time, and the value of e is not fixed for a material.
09

Summary

In one line. A collision is described by the masses, the velocities and how elastic it is, and the panels compare two totals before and after.

Key points

  • Σp is the same before and after every collision, in every frame.
  • ΣKE is conserved only when e = 1. At e = 0 the carts stick and the loss is greatest.
  • An explosion starts with Σp = 0 and turns the stored energy Q into ΣKE.
  • ΔKE is the same in every frame, and vb = vcm gives the frame where Σp = 0.

Common mix-ups

  • "If kinetic energy disappears when objects stick, momentum must disappear too." Only kinetic energy is lost. Σp is unchanged.
  • "Σp has one value that every observer agrees on." Its value depends on the frame. Only the equality before and after holds in all of them.
  • "A moving cart always stops dead in an elastic collision." It stops only when the other cart is at rest and has the same mass.

Things to try on your own

  • Choose any masses and velocities, work out Σp by hand, and compare it with the table.
  • Sweep e from 0 to 1 and compare ΔKE with −½μ(1 − e²)(v₁ − v₂)² at a few values.
  • Pick unequal masses, stick them, then set vb to vcm and check that both carts end at rest.
